result.rationale:
Both plans treat this as a cross-sectional broad-effect question, which is the right reading — the firm is asking whether call tone is a usable input at all, not pitching one name. From there the plans diverge on feasibility and sequencing.

Plan A is a beautifully specified academic paper written for a firm with engineers, a data science team, and a research infrastructure: continued MLM pretraining on ~2B transcript tokens with deberta-v3-large, a 6,000-sentence dual-annotator labelling program with Krippendorff alpha targets, 150k LLM silver labels, seven-way ablation ladders, TAQ time-weighted spreads, Markit borrow data, capacity curves and deflated Sharpe. There is no one at this firm who can build it, no one who can maintain it, and no one on the investment committee who can evaluate it. The stated constraint — 'defensible to an investment committee that is skeptical of models it cannot inspect' — is directly violated by a fine-tuned encoder whose tone score is a probability aggregate nobody can trace. It also imports the wrong firm's kill risks: capacity, borrow cost, break-even bps and crowding as a 'primary result' are the concerns of a systematic book, not of a manager whose failure mode is being wrong about a business. And every stage is a prerequisite for the next: the domain-adaptive pretraining and annotation program must be finished before any return test exists, so the plan cannot be stopped at week four with anything learned.

Plan B starts with the simplest thing that could resolve the question — Loughran-McDonald counts on management Q&A turns, differenced within firm — and puts the decisive test at the front. It gets to a pooled panel result with an incremental t-statistic by day 10, has a pre-committed, dated specification before touching returns (which genuinely constrains researcher degrees of freedom rather than merely mentioning multiple testing), and four explicit numeric kill thresholds including 'a t of 2.1 is a kill.' The complexity budget is spent only after the gate passes. Crucially, the half day of vendor calls is the best edge work in either plan: if S&P, MarketPsych or RavenPack already sell this score to hundreds of clients, the idea is dead on arrival, and the rank-correlation-above-0.7 test makes 'commodity duplication' a falsifiable outcome rather than a caveat. The 2004-2010 replication plus decay prior is an honest attempt to establish what is incremental versus published, and the placebo over [-63,-3] and shuffled-speaker-label test are checks that can actually fail. Plan A's placebo list is longer but its edge question — does anyone already know this — is left to a pitfalls bullet.

On evidence standard, Type I dominates for a concentrated book, and Plan B's bar (clustered t≥2.5 with Bonferroni escalation, sign in 7 of 10 years, robustness across size quartiles, net spread and IR floors) is demanding without being unreachable. Plan A's Harvey-Liu-Zhu t>3 is defensible too, but it buys that rigour at a cost the firm cannot pay.

Both plans share a horizon problem for a 3-5 year holder, and Plan B's day 11-14 mention of 'latency and capacity' is a stray systematic-firm concern. Neither is disqualifying relative to the gap in executability. I would put the analyst on Plan B, and if it passes the gate, the natural follow-on for this firm is licensing a vendor score or using tone qualitatively in the existing fundamental process — not building Plan A.

This is a $400M fundamental shop on Bloomberg and Excel, two analysts, no engineers, no database, and an IC hostile to models it cannot inspect. Plan B was written for a systematic quant firm with a GPU budget and a research engineering team: ~2B-token domain-adaptive masked LM pretraining, dual-head encoder, two-annotator gold sets plus 150k LLM silver labels, per-speaker embedding-cosine evasion measures, TAQ time-weighted spreads, Markit borrow, capacity-where-net-alpha-halves. None of that can be executed by one analyst here, none of it can be maintained, and the headline output would rest on a pipeline nobody at the firm can inspect or reproduce — exactly the thing the IC rejects. Plan B's preoccupations (borrow cost, break-even bps, crowding, alpha decay, managers writing for machines) are the right worries for a book that lives on capacity and cost; they are the wrong worries for a firm whose stated failure mode is being wrong about a business.

Plan A is sized to the actual constraint. It uses the simplest measure that could resolve the question — Loughran-McDonald counts on parsed management Q&A turns, differenced within firm — which is arithmetic an analyst can show the IC in a spreadsheet and which the committee can gut-check. One primary specification, frozen before returns are touched, with pre-committed kill thresholds and an explicit statement that a t of 2.1 is a kill. That is the right burden of proof for a concentrated book that cannot diversify away a false positive: Type I dominates, and Plan A's Bonferroni bump plus year-by-year sign consistency plus size-quintile robustness is a demanding but cheap standard. Plan B's t>3.0 and deflated Sharpe are equally demanding but arrive after months of machinery whose researcher degrees of freedom are far larger than its formal gate acknowledges.

Neither plan invents economics; both state kill criteria honestly and both admit a clean null is an output. result.key_differentiator: Plan A puts the one cheap, spreadsheet-only test that can kill the whole premise (Rule 605 wholesaler reports plus FINRA MPID data) first and pre-commits to stopping there, whereas Plan B buries the identification question inside a full systematic long-short signal build that this five-person, no-engineer, 3-5-year-horizon shop could never run, staff, or defend.
result.rationale:
Neither plan is a natural fit for a $400M concentrated long-only manager on Bloomberg and Excel — this is a microstructure question the firm probably should not be asking — so the decision turns on which plan can produce something useful before the infrastructure requirement bites, and which one is answering a question this firm could act on.

Plan A splits the question into its two real claims and refuses to build a signal until claim (1) — does round-lot size actually identify retail origination — survives. Its first step is Benchmark C: Rule 605 wholesaler execution reports broken out by odd-lot/fractional/dollar buckets, plus FINRA OTC transparency by MPID. That is genuinely free, genuinely Excel-executable by one analyst, genuinely inspectable by a skeptical IC, and it is explicitly designated as the step that alone can kill the project. Plan A also states H0 as its own prior with an economic story (retail has migrated to dollar/fractional orders arriving as odd or mixed lots, while VWAP/TWAP schedulers slice into 100-share children, making round lots closer to an institutional signature). If that is right — and it likely is — the firm learns in a week or two that the premise is dead, and the deliverable is a negative result plus a map of better retail identifiers. Killing this early is exactly the right outcome for a shop with two analysts. Plan A's mechanism tests (round-notional clustering at $100/$500/$1,000 versus round-share clustering; price-elasticity of round-lot frequency) are the kind of crude, entropy-reducing checks that separate 'retail behavioral signature' from 'algo slicing artifact,' and they are checks an IC can follow verbally.

Plan A also correctly identifies the circularity risk that Plan B soft-pedals: round-lot imbalance can predict returns mechanically through generic order-flow imbalance with no retail content whatsoever, so backtesting first and retrofitting the retail story is backwards.

Plan B is a competent quant equity research plan written for a different firm. It assumes WRDS, TAQ tick cleaning per Holden-Jacobsen, Markit or Ortex borrow fees, Fama-MacBeth with Newey-West cross-checked against Hansen-Hodrick and block bootstrap, a square-root impact model with three k calibrations, and a sensitivity grid across signing algorithm, NBBO lag, scaling, smoothing, weighting and decile count. Its output is a daily-rebalanced, beta-neutral, dollar-neutral long-short book with a five-day holding period. This firm holds 25-30 names for three to five years and has no one to maintain a database; the horizon mismatch is total and the infrastructure requirement is unbuildable. The capacity analysis across $50M-$5B AUM is a number produced for a fund that does not exist here, and it anchors sizing on a book the firm cannot run. Nothing in Plan B is inspectable before the end; there is no cheap early gate and no branch that gets dropped.

Plan B's falsification is also weaker than it looks in one specific place: 'a positive 20-day coefficient is reinterpreted, not failure' converts a sign flip from disconfirmation into narrative flexibility. Combined with the size of the sensitivity grid, that is a lot of researcher degrees of freedom in a design whose primary risk it already concedes is that the result is short-term reversal relabeled.

Plan A is far from clean — the tiered-round-lot recomputation, exchange proprietary RLP feeds, Hui-Walter latent-class estimation and DuckDB/Spark partitioning are all beyond this firm, and its five sequential kill gates with pre-registered thresholds and Benjamini-Hochberg are more machinery than the question needs. Its Phase 2 after-cost Sharpe gate of 1.0 is a criterion for a fund that cannot exist here. But all of that sits behind a free first step that will most likely stop the work, and that is the difference that matters.

result.key_differentiator: Plan B produces a cross-episode, feature-coded base rate with a genuine out-of-sample holdout and mechanism-derived negative controls — something 200 quants and a replication committee can re-run and turn into a cross-sectional signal — whereas Plan A produces a bespoke single-name valuation model with hand-set haircuts that this firm cannot replicate, trade, or generalize.
result.rationale:
The question as posed to a systematic firm is not 'what is this one company worth' but 'is shortage guidance a repeatable predictor of contract-backed revenue durability, and is that already priced.' Plan A answers the first question: a forward revenue bridge, an agreement register, a reverse DCF, EV/haircut-adjusted committed gross profit, and a constructive/negative threshold list. That output is an investment-committee memo for a concentrated long-only shop. It is not something a research platform can replicate — the entire result hinges on analyst-assigned Tier 1/2/3 haircuts (90-95%, 70%, 25-35%) and pass/fail thresholds (60% NTM coverage, 45% top-3 share, 2-year horizon gap) that are asserted rather than estimated. Plan A's only breadth is a four-episode 'backtest' appended at the end, after all the modeling machinery — exactly backwards: the historical base rate is the check that determines whether the bespoke model is worth building at all.

Plan B is built the way this firm reasons. It defines the event mechanically at first allocation-language filing via EDGAR, keeps every episode regardless of outcome, codes contract features and outcomes on an ordinal scale separating price from volume, and reports conditional base rates by feature rather than regressing a 25-observation sample into false precision — the right evidence standard for a setting where cross-sectional significance was never available. It builds the framework on most episodes, holds out the 2021-24 auto-semi cycle, and predicts it with dates before checking. It derives from its own mechanism where the effect should be absent — aerospace forgings and LNG should hold, MLCC and container slots should break, ordered by qualification lag not contract label — and treats that as the test. It states a falsifier that would kill the hypothesis (contracted price above spot for 8+ quarters absent a qualification moat). And it pre-registers 3-5 checkable predictions on the live HBM case with a 12-month clock, so the work generates forward evidence rather than only backward description. Where sources disagree, shipment data wins — a stated arbitration rule, not a hope.

On edge: B's variant view is explicit and contrarian — LTAs honored in volume, broken in price; a large disclosed LTA book as a coincident cycle-peak indicator; prepayments funding the capacity that destroys pricing. That is a diff against the consensus 'duration story deserving a higher multiple' the plan names in its first line. A's prior is similar in spirit but is resolved by a valuation exercise on one name rather than by evidence that generalizes. On invented economics, B is the more disciplined: its output is an explicitly probability-weighted haircut with a statement of what would justify the multiple, not a number. A's tier haircuts and threshold grid are precise figures with only loose calibration behind them, and they will anchor sizing.

Both plans miss the firm's actual scoreboard — neither measures forward returns net of costs, capacity, or crowding, and both work on quarterly horizons against a days-to-weeks book. That is a real defect in both, and it partly reflects a question whose signature does not match the firm. But B's output is the one that can be extended into a cross-sectional signal: an event definition, a feature vector, a coded outcome, and base rates by feature are one step from a tradeable specification. A's output is a single EV comparison that cannot be.
issues_with_winner: Horizon is T+4/8/12 quarters against a days-to-weeks book; the plan never states how a contract-outcome base rate becomes a tradeable signal, and never touches transaction costs, capacity, or crowding — the firm's stated pass/fail criteria.
Measures contract price/volume outcomes, not stock returns; the proxy-to-P&L link is asserted by the framing rather than tested even once.

Commits to a lot of licensed data (TrendForce, Fastmarkets, UxC, Argus/ICIS, Drewry/Xeneta, Panjiva, PACER) before any cheap version has shown the base rate separates; a free-proxy pass on three or four episodes could have killed or confirmed the price-versus-volume split first.

25-ish episodes with conditional base rates cut by four features leaves cells of two or three; the plan says 'ranked not regressed,' which is honest, but does not state how many episodes per cell it needs before it will report a rate.

No early kill gate. The falsifier is defined but sits at the end of the framework build; hand-coding Exhibit 10 contracts and building capacity ledgers per market is weeks of work before the first judgeable output.
Adaptivity is thin — it says what would falsify the hypothesis but not which branches get dropped if, say, the qualification-lag split fails to order the episodes.
issues_with_loser: Answers a single-name valuation question for a systematic firm whose research committee re-runs results independently; the tier haircuts, six-attribute scores, and adversarial transcript reads are irreproducible analyst judgment.

Threshold grid and haircut ladder are invented magnitudes — 90-95%/70%/25-35%, 60% NTM coverage, 15% cash support, 2-year horizon gap — asserted as if calibrated, and they will anchor position sizing.

Sequenced backwards: the historical episode base rate that would determine whether shortage guidance means anything at all is appended as 'validation' after the entire bridge, register, scenario and reverse-DCF machinery is built.
No cross-sectional breadth and no negative controls derived from a mechanism — no statement of where the lock-in effect should fail to appear.

Enormous machinery (RPO roll-forward with cancellations as a plug, 10-15 year depreciation schedules, three full scenario paths) for a question the firm would resolve with an event study; every extra stage adds degrees of freedom and none is shown to be necessary.
Output is EV/haircut-adjusted committed gross profit versus a reverse DCF — not a form this firm can trade, size, or capacity-check.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A builds a cross-episode, base-rate framework with mechanism-derived negative controls and a pre-committed holdout — the only output form a 200-researcher systematic shop can independently re-run and eventually turn into a cross-sectional signal — whereas Plan B is a single-name accounting valuation whose verdict rests on hand-set thresholds nobody can replicate.
result.rationale:
Neither plan is a natural fit: the question arrives at a systematic firm with a days-to-weeks horizon, and both plans reason in quarters and years, neither measures returns net of cost, and neither asks whether the 'shortage guidance implies durable revenue' narrative is already crowded or vendor-supplied. So the choice is which misfit is closer to something this firm can use and re-run.

Plan A is structured as an event study across 20-30 episodes with a machine-findable T=0 (first allocation-language filing in EDGAR), an explicit coding scheme, ranked conditional base rates rather than an over-parameterized regression on tiny N, a genuine holdout (build on everything except 2021-24 auto semis, then predict the holdout with dates before looking), and pre-registered checks on the live HBM case. Most importantly it derives from its own mechanism where the effect should be absent: aerospace forgings and LNG SPAs should hold, MLCC and container slots should break, ordered by requalification lag rather than by contract label. That is a real negative control, and it directly attacks the premise inherited from the question rather than assuming it. Its secondary hypothesis — a large disclosed LTA book as a coincident cycle-peak marker — is exactly the kind of variant, contrarian, cross-sectionally testable claim this firm can take to a research committee and later convert into a signal. It also refuses to manufacture a P&L number: the output is a probability-weighted haircut plus a statement of what would justify the multiple.

Plan B is the better piece of fundamental accounting work and would win at a concentrated long-only shop. It knows more about ASC 606 mechanics, and its reverse DCF at least asks what the market already prices, which is a real edge check Plan A only gestures at. But almost everything decisive in it is unreplicable judgment: Tier haircuts of 90-95/70/25-35 percent, and a constructive gate requiring simultaneously >=60% NTM Tier 1/2 coverage, >=40% year-two, >=15% cash support, <45% top-3 concentration, >=50% mirror reconciliation and a modeled horizon >=2 years beyond market-implied. Those numbers are asserted, not derived from anything the plan produces, and a conjunctive six-condition gate is precisely the Type II-expensive design a breadth-oriented systematic firm should avoid — almost no real case clears all six, and a research committee cannot re-derive any of the cut points. The RPO roll-forward that solves net bookings as a plug and then backs out cancellations is a lot of derived-from-derived arithmetic before anything judgeable emerges, and the plan's only cross-episode work (four episodes, descriptive) sits at the end as validation rather than at the front as the test of whether the premise holds at all.

Sequencing and steerability also favor A: coding contracts and outcomes produces inspectable intermediate artifacts (a hand-checkable sample of coded episodes, base rates by feature) early, and it names a specific falsifier — contracted price materially above spot for 8+ quarters post-normalization absent a qualification moat — that would kill the hypothesis. Plan B's pitfalls list names enforcement weakness and reflexivity and then proceeds to a coverage ratio that treats take-or-pay damages as a scoring attribute anyway.
issues_with_winner: Never measures returns: no test of whether shortage guidance or LTA disclosure predicts price, no transaction-cost, capacity or crowding analysis — the three things this firm actually judges work on.
Outcome horizon of T+4/8/12 quarters is far outside the stated days-to-weeks holding period; the bridge from base rates to a tradable signal is left unbuilt.

N of 20-30 heterogeneous episodes across polysilicon, semis, LNG, shipping and uranium; pooling is defensible for base rates but the conditional cuts by feature will have handfuls of observations each and no stated way to judge whether a rate difference is meaningful beyond ordering.

Contract coding across Exhibit 10 filings, PACER and foreign arbitration records is heavy manual work; it is AI-tractable but the plan does not specify a hand-checked sample or coverage-by-period audit.
Edge is only implicit — it asserts the market reads this as a duration story but does not diff against sell-side estimate revisions or positioning.
issues_with_loser: Tier haircuts (90-95%, 70%, 25-35%) and the entire threshold battery (>=60%, >=40%, >=15%, <45%, >=50%, >=2 years) are asserted magnitudes that nothing in the plan derives; they would anchor a decision on fabricated numbers.
Conjunctive six-condition constructive gate is tight enough to reject nearly every real case — a Type II cost, not a virtue, at a firm that needs breadth.
Output is a single-name valuation verdict (EV vs haircut-adjusted committed gross profit, reverse DCF) that a systematic research committee cannot independently re-run.

Decisive question — does shortage guidance historically portend durable revenue and returns — is deferred to a four-episode backtest at the end, after all the accounting machinery; the cheap test that could kill the idea is last.
No mechanism-derived negative controls: nothing states where the lock-in effect should be absent, so the framework cannot fail.
RPO roll-forward solving net bookings as a plug and backing out cancellations from book-to-bill stacks inference on inference with many free parameters.
